pitfall_name: JS↔WASM boundary copies on every field element or proof chunk
what_happens: Proving time appears 2-5× slower than native; heap profiles show massive ArrayBuffer allocation/churn even though the WASM module itself is stable.
why: Passing a JS TypedArray into a WASM function that takes a pointer still incurs a copy unless the buffer is explicitly transferred or the WASM linear memory is used in-place; crypto kernels that cross the boundary per limb or per constraint amplify the cost.
how_discovered: Performance counters or browser memory timeline show allocation rate proportional to proof size rather than constant; typically wastes 1-3 days chasing 'slow field arithmetic'.
mitigation: Allocate once in WASM memory, keep all intermediate field elements and witness data inside linear memory, and only marshal the final proof bytes out; use Memory views or wasm-bindgen zero-copy patterns.

pitfall_name: SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation and is still blocked in many embedding contexts
what_happens: WASM threads or Atomics simply throw or fall back to single-threaded; multi-threaded proving silently becomes single-core.
why: Browsers gate SharedArrayBuffer behind COOP/COEP headers (crossOriginIsolated === true). Iframes, many CDN setups, and older enterprise proxies strip or omit the headers; Safari had longer restrictions.
how_discovered: navigator.crossOriginIsolated is false while the code assumes threads; or Atomics.wait throws; often discovered only after deploying to production domain, wasting days.
mitigation: Serve with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (or credentialless); detect crossOriginIsolated at startup and fall back gracefully; avoid relying on SAB inside third-party iframes.

pitfall_name: WASM 32-bit linear memory ceiling and growth failure under large circuits
what_happens: Memory.grow returns -1 or the module traps once the heap approaches 2-4 GiB; proving of large circuits aborts mid-run.
why: Standard WASM is 32-bit addressed (max ~4 GiB, practical browser limits often lower due to contiguous reservation). Proving systems that allocate large FFTs, quotient polynomials, or full witness tables hit the wall; browsers may also refuse growth under memory pressure.
how_discovered: Sudden trap or OOM after working on smaller instances; memory timeline shows growth attempts failing; wastes hours to a day diagnosing 'random' crashes.
mitigation: Stream or chunk large polynomials, reuse buffers aggressively, prefer memory64 where available (still limited support), or offload the largest allocations to WebGPU buffers.

pitfall_name: WASM SIMD not vectorizing the actual field arithmetic
what_happens: Binary contains SIMD opcodes and 'SIMD enabled' flags are set, yet cycle counts or throughput match scalar code.
why: LLVM/Binaryen SIMD lowering is sensitive to lane widths, alignment, and the exact integer widths used in Montgomery or goldilocks arithmetic; many hand-written or macro-generated field implementations stay scalar because the autovectorizer cannot see through the carry chains or modular reductions.
how_discovered: objdump / wasm-objdump shows few or no v128 operations inside the hot mul/reduce loops; or micro-benchmarks of the field mul show no speedup vs scalar build; typically wastes 1-2 days of 'why is SIMD not helping'.
mitigation: Inspect the generated WASM for v128 in the critical kernels; rewrite hot paths with explicit SIMD intrinsics or platform-specific primitives that the compiler respects; verify with a disassembly diff.

pitfall_name: WebGPU buffer mapAsync / readback stalls counted as GPU compute time
what_happens: Reported GPU proving time includes long stalls; throughput looks far below theoretical shader occupancy.
why: mapAsync is asynchronous from the JS side but the GPU timeline still serializes the readback; if the measurement bracket includes the await on the mapped range, host-side copy and synchronization are attributed to the kernel.
how_discovered: Timestamp queries or GPU duration timestamps show much smaller numbers than the wall-clock bracket around mapAsync; or CPU profiles show the main thread blocked in the await; often wastes a day of 'GPU is slow' investigation.
mitigation: Use timestamp queries around the compute pass only; keep readback outside the timed region; prefer double-buffering so the next dispatch proceeds while the previous result is mapped.

pitfall_name: GPU timestamp-query support is optional and quantization is coarse
what_happens: Timing code throws or returns zeros; or reported kernel times have 1-10 µs steps that swamp short dispatches.
why: timestamp-query is a WebGPU feature level that many mobile and some desktop adapters still lack; even when present, the resolution is adapter-dependent and often coarser than CPU timers, so short MSM or NTT kernels are dominated by quantization noise.
how_discovered: adapter.features missing 'timestamp-query' or values that are identical across runs of different sizes; wastes hours before falling back to coarser measurement.
mitigation: Feature-detect and fall back to CPU wall time around queue.submit + onSubmittedWorkDone; batch enough work that quantization becomes negligible; never treat a single short dispatch time as authoritative.

pitfall_name: Browser timer clamping and cross-origin isolation effects on performance.now
what_happens: Benchmark numbers become quantized to 1 ms or 100 µs; short iterations appear identical; speed-ups disappear.
why: Without cross-origin isolation, many browsers clamp performance.now to 1 ms or coarser for fingerprinting resistance; even with isolation the resolution is not guaranteed to be nanosecond. Measurement of sub-millisecond field operations or small proofs is therefore distorted.
how_discovered: All iteration times are multiples of 1 ms or show zero variance; comparing isolated vs non-isolated origins reveals the clamp; typically wastes half a day of 'why are my micro-benchmarks flat'.
mitigation: Ensure COOP/COEP so crossOriginIsolated is true; measure longer batches (many proofs or large circuits) so clamping error is amortized; prefer GPU timestamp queries when available.

what_happens: First few proofs are dramatically slower; later proofs suddenly speed up, so average or 'peak' numbers depend on how many iterations were discarded.
why: JS and the WASM baseline compiler start slow; optimizing tiers (TurboFan, etc.) recompile hot functions after a threshold of invocations. If the benchmark loop itself triggers tier-up, the measured interval mixes cold and hot code.
how_discovered: Time-per-proof curve shows a clear step function after N iterations; disabling the optimizing compiler (or using --no-opt flags in controlled environments) removes the step; wastes a day of unstable numbers.
mitigation: Run a fixed, sufficiently long warmup that is discarded; measure only after steady-state; or pin to a known tier if the engine exposes flags (not available to normal web content).

pitfall_name: GC pauses and minor collections attributed to the proving kernel
what_happens: Occasional multi-millisecond spikes in an otherwise smooth proving timeline; throughput variance is high.
why: Even when most data lives in WASM memory, any JS-side TypedArray views, temporary proof objects, or logging allocate on the JS heap; major GC or growing nursery pauses are charged to the surrounding wall-clock measurement.
how_discovered: Browser performance timeline shows yellow/gray GC bars exactly at the spikes; allocating less on the JS side removes them; often mis-diagnosed as 'WASM GC' or scheduler noise for hours.
mitigation: Keep allocation off the hot path; reuse JS objects; force a GC before timed runs if the engine allows (chrome://tracing or equivalent); measure with allocation instrumentation.

pitfall_name: Mobile browser memory kills and background tab throttling
what_happens: Tab is discarded or process is killed mid-proof; or proving slows by 5-10× when the phone screen turns off or the tab is backgrounded.
why: Mobile OSes aggressively reclaim memory from background tabs; browsers also throttle timers and JS execution. Large WASM heaps + WebGPU resources exceed the per-tab budget on mid-range devices.
how_discovered: Proofs that finish on desktop die on phone; visibilitychange or freeze events correlate with kills; wastes days of 'works on my laptop' debugging.
mitigation: Detect deviceMemory / hardwareConcurrency and shrink circuit or switch to a lighter proving mode; listen for visibilitychange and checkpoint; keep working set under typical mobile limits (~300-600 MB).

pitfall_name: Safari WebGPU and WASM thread divergences
what_happens: Code that runs on Chrome/Firefox fails or is dramatically slower on Safari; timestamp queries or certain buffer usages are missing; threads may be limited.
why: Safari's WebGPU implementation lagged in feature completeness (timestamp-query, certain storage-texture usages) and its WASM threading / SAB story has historically been more restrictive; scheduler and memory allocator behavior also differ under pressure.
how_discovered: Feature detection fails only on Safari; or proofs that pass elsewhere OOM or time out; typically discovered late in cross-browser testing, wasting 1-2 days.
mitigation: Feature-detect every WebGPU capability used; maintain a Safari-specific reduced path; test on real Safari early; do not assume Chrome behavior is universal.

pitfall_name: Iframe and embedded-context restrictions on workers, SAB, and WebGPU
what_happens: Proving that works in a top-level page fails when embedded; workers cannot be created or SharedArrayBuffer is unavailable; WebGPU adapter request returns null.
why: Cross-origin iframes inherit stricter isolation; COOP/COEP must be set on both the embedder and the embeddee; some browsers further restrict WebGPU and high-resolution timers inside iframes for fingerprinting and security reasons.
how_discovered: Same origin works top-level but fails when loaded as an iframe in a host application; wastes a day of 'it works locally' confusion.
mitigation: Require top-level or carefully coordinated COOP/COEP on the whole frame chain; detect the embedding context and surface a clear error; prefer popup or dedicated origin for heavy proving.
